summary: The paper argues that special-purpose systems can avoid I/O limits when each data item fetched from memory is reused as it moves through a pipeline of simple processing cells. It illustrates the idea with a family of convolution array designs that differ in which operands stay in cells and which are broadcast, fanned in or streamed, and compares them by I/O needs, cell utilization and wiring.
why_read: It is the foundational statement of systolic architecture and explains why regular cell-to-cell data flow cuts memory traffic for compute-bound problems.
main_contribution: A design principle for systolic arrays, shown through a family of convolution designs that compare which operands stay in cells and which move.
main_limitation: The designs are worked out by hand for regular compute-bound problems, and the paper states that their automatic design is still an open question.
evaluation_method: analytic argument and qualitative comparison of designs; no experiments
